distribute.n: To distribute something is to give out or spread it among a number of people, places or recipients, usually in shares or in an organised way. Typical objects are food, aid, leaflets, profits, tickets and software; the usual pattern is distribute something to people or among them. Distribute is close to share out and hand out, but it suggests larger quantities and a deliberate plan. The noun is distribution, and a distributor is a company that supplies shops.
x: The charity distributes warm blankets to homeless people every winter.
Profits are distributed among all the members of the cooperative.
Volunteers distributed leaflets outside the station.

sphere.n: A sphere is either a perfectly round three-dimensional shape, like a ball, or a particular area of activity, interest or influence. In the second sense it appears in set phrases such as the public sphere, the private sphere and sphere of influence, and in the pattern in the sphere of politics. Sphere of life is broader and more abstract than the near-synonym field, and it fits well in writing about society, power and international relations.
x: The artist painted a glass sphere floating above the sea.
Education falls within the sphere of local government.
Each country tried to widen its sphere of influence in the region.

capable.n: If someone or something is capable, they have the ability or the qualities needed to do something. The most common pattern is capable of plus a noun or an -ing form, as in capable of winning. Used alone before a noun, it means skilled and reliable: a capable manager. Capable is close to able, but able takes a to-infinitive (able to swim), while capable takes of. The opposite is incapable, and the noun is capability.
x: She is a capable engineer who can solve almost any technical problem.
The new battery is capable of powering a phone for three days.
I know you are capable of better work than this.

demonstrate.n: To demonstrate something is to show clearly, with evidence or an example, that it is true or that it works. It is used with studies, experiments, results and people showing a skill or quality, often in the patterns demonstrate that or demonstrate how. Demonstrate is stronger and more careful than show, and it is common in academic writing. It also means to show a product in use, and to take part in a protest march. The noun is demonstration.
x: The experiment demonstrates that plants grow faster in blue light.
The chef demonstrated how to fold the dough.
Thousands of people demonstrated outside parliament against the new law.

prime.n: As an adjective, prime means main, most important or of the very best quality. It comes before the noun in fixed combinations: a prime example, prime suspect, prime location, prime minister and prime time. A prime example is a clear, typical illustration, while a prime suspect is the person police think most likely guilty. Prime is stronger than main and often suggests the best, as in prime beef. In maths, a prime number divides only by one and itself.
x: The old harbour is a prime location for a new restaurant.
Police named him as their prime suspect.
The museum is a prime example of Art Deco architecture.

simulate.n: To simulate something is to create conditions, usually with a computer or a model, that copy a real process closely enough for study, testing or training. Typical objects are conditions, weather, flights, behaviour and attacks. Simulate suggests a careful, technical copy, while pretend and fake suggest deception. A related meaning is to imitate the look of something, as in simulated leather. The noun is simulation, and a flight simulator is the machine used by trainee pilots.
x: Engineers simulate earthquakes to test how tall buildings will react.
The training programme simulates real emergencies for new nurses.
The software simulated the spread of the disease across the country.

identical.n: If two things are identical, they are exactly the same in every detail, with no difference at all. The usual pattern is identical to something or identical in something, and the phrase identical twins refers to twins from one egg who look alike. Identical is stronger than similar, which allows small differences, and close to the same, which is more informal. It is not normally used with very, because exact sameness has no degrees; almost identical works instead.
x: The two houses look identical from the street.
Her answer was identical to the one on the website.
Identical twins share the same genes.

input.n: As a noun, input means the ideas, advice, effort or material that people or things put into a project or process. It is usually uncountable: with input from experts, valuable input, public input. In computing it means the data or commands entered into a system, and its opposite is output. Input is close to contribution, but it also suggests the opinions people are asked for before a decision. As a verb, it means to enter data, with the forms input or inputted.
x: The manager asked the whole team for input before changing the schedule.
The software needs input from a keyboard or a microphone.
Parents had no input into the new school rules.

visual.n: Visual describes anything connected with seeing or sight, or something that can be seen rather than heard or read. It is common in visual aid, visual arts, visual impact, visual effects and visual learner. Visual is the general word, while optical often relates to light and lenses, as in optical illusion. As a noun, visuals means pictures, charts or video used to illustrate something. The adverb is visually, as in visually impaired or visually striking.
x: The film is famous for its stunning visual effects.
Many children are visual learners who remember pictures better than words.
Add a few visuals to your presentation to keep the audience interested.

cease.n: To cease is to stop happening, or to bring something to an end. It is a fairly formal verb found in news, law and business: cease to exist, cease trading, cease production. It can take an -ing form or a to-infinitive: cease operating or cease to operate. Cease is more official than stop, and it often suggests a final ending rather than a pause. A ceasefire is an agreement to stop fighting, and ceaseless means continuing without end.
x: The company ceased trading last month after years of losses.
The noise ceased as suddenly as it had begun.
Under the agreement, both armies must cease fire at midnight.

entity.n: An entity is something that exists as a separate unit with its own identity, whether it is a physical thing, an organisation or an idea. It is most common in legal and business English: a legal entity, a separate entity, a corporate entity, a government entity. Entity is a deliberately general word, used when the exact type of thing is unclear or not important. A company counts as a legal entity because the law treats it like a person for contracts and debts.
x: The charity is a legal entity separate from its founders.
Scientists once thought the two species were one entity.
Each department is treated as an independent entity within the group.

exhibit.n: As a verb, exhibit has two main meanings. It can mean to show something to the public, such as art, products or animals at a gallery or fair. It can also mean to display a quality, sign or behaviour, as in exhibit symptoms or exhibit courage. This second use is common in science and medicine. Exhibit is more formal than show. As a noun, an exhibit is an object displayed in a museum, or evidence presented in a court.
x: The gallery will exhibit her paintings throughout the summer.
Several of the children exhibited symptoms of the flu.
The suspect exhibited no sign of remorse.

sum.n: A sum is an amount of money, as in a large sum of money, or the total you get when you add numbers together. In the money sense it is usually modified by an adjective: a considerable sum, a small sum, a lump sum. In British English, sums can also mean simple arithmetic problems done by children. The phrase in sum means in summary, and the verb sum up means to give the main points.
x: She paid a substantial sum for the vintage car.
The sum of three and four is seven.
He received a lump sum when he retired.

thereby.n: Thereby is an adverb meaning as a result of the action just mentioned, or by that means. It usually comes before an -ing form: they cut costs, thereby saving jobs. It links one action to its consequence in a single sentence and is typical of written, academic or business English. Thereby is a compact alternative to as a result or which means that. It is not usually used in casual speech, where so or this way sound more natural.
x: The firm switched to solar power, thereby cutting its energy bills in half.
She learned Spanish at night, thereby improving her chances of promotion.
Regular exercise strengthens the heart, thereby reducing the risk of disease.

transmit.n: To transmit something is to send or pass it from one person or place to another. It is used for signals, data, programmes, news and diseases: transmit data, transmit a signal, transmit a virus. Transmit is more technical than send and is normal in broadcasting, telecommunications and medicine. It also covers passing on qualities or knowledge, as in values transmitted from parent to child. The noun is transmission, and a transmitter is the device that sends signals.
x: The satellite transmits live pictures to stations around the world.
Mosquitoes can transmit several serious diseases.
Stories were transmitted from generation to generation by word of mouth.

successor.n: A successor is the person or thing that comes after another and takes over their role, position or place. The usual pattern is successor to someone or something, as in her successor as director. Typical collocations are natural successor, chosen successor and worthy successor. For products, a successor is the newer model that replaces an older one. The opposite is predecessor, and the verb is succeed, which also means to take over a job or throne.
x: The president has not yet named a successor.
The new phone is the successor to last year's popular model.
He was seen as the natural successor to the retiring headmaster.

exploit.n: To exploit has two sides. Neutrally, it means to use something fully and effectively, especially a resource or opportunity: exploit natural resources, exploit a weakness. Negatively, it means to treat people unfairly in order to gain from them, as in exploit workers or exploit children. Context shows which meaning is intended. Exploit is stronger than use and often carries criticism. The noun exploitation has the same split, and an exploit can also be a bold, daring act.
x: Wind farms exploit the strong winds along the coast.
Hackers exploited a flaw in the website to steal data.
Some employers exploit young workers by paying them very little.

precise.n: Precise means exact and accurate in detail, with no mistakes or vagueness. It is common with details, measurements, instructions, timing and definitions: precise location, precise figure, a precise moment. To be precise is a phrase used to add an exact detail, and at that precise moment stresses the exact time. Precise is close to exact; it often suggests careful, fine accuracy, and it can also describe a careful person. The noun is precision and the adverb is precisely.
x: Please give me precise directions, because the village is hard to find.
The recipe requires precise measurements.
It was ten years ago, eleven to be precise.

trace.n: As a verb, trace means to find the origin, cause or history of something by following clues. It is often used with back or to: trace the problem back to a faulty cable, trace a call, trace ancestors. It also means to copy a drawing by following its lines on thin paper. Trace is more investigative than find and suggests following a path step by step. As a noun, a trace is a small sign that something existed, as in no trace of the missing hikers.
x: Investigators traced the money to an account in another country.
She traced her family history back to the sixteenth century.
The engineer traced the fault to a loose wire.

pollinator.n: A pollinator is an animal, most often a bee, butterfly, moth, bat or bird, that carries pollen from one flower to another and so helps plants produce seeds and fruit. It appears in phrases such as wild pollinator, insect pollinator and decline of pollinators, and often in articles about farming and the environment. The verb is pollinate, and the process is pollination. Pollinator is a more precise word than insect because many pollinators are not insects.
x: Many crops depend on wild pollinators such as bumblebees.
Pesticides are one reason pollinators are declining in Europe.
Hummingbirds are important pollinators of tropical flowers.
